title: The Explorer's Daughter
author: Kari Herbert
blurb: Watching a narwhal hunt in Greenland, Herbert weighs childhood memories against an adult understanding of Arctic survival.
source: Herbert writes about her experience watching a narwhal hunt in the Arctic
heading: The Explorer's Daughter - Kari Herbert
context: As a small child, Herbert lived, with her family, among the Inughuit people (sometimes called Inuits, or Eskimos) in the harsh environment of the Arctic. In 2002 she revisited the area, staying near Thule, a remote settlement in North Greenland. In this passage she writes about her experience of watching a hunt for the narwhal, a toothed whale, and what she thought and felt about it.

paragraphs.html: Two hours after the last of the hunters had returned and eaten, narwhal were spotted again, this time very close. Within an hour even those of us on shore could with the naked eye see the plumes of spray from the narwhal catching the light in a spectral play of colour. Two large pods of narwhal circled in the fjord, often looking as if they were going to merge, but always slowly, methodically passing each other by. Scrambling back up to the lookout I looked across the glittering kingdom in front of me and took a sharp intake of breath. The hunters were dotted all around the fjord. The evening light was turning butter-gold, glinting off man and whale and catching the soft billows of smoke from a lone hunter's pipe. From where we sat at the lookout it looked as though the hunters were close enough to touch the narwhal with their bare hands and yet they never moved. Distances are always deceptive in the Arctic, and I fell to wondering if the narwhal existed at all or were instead mischievous tricks of the shifting light. ...

The narwhal rarely stray from High Arctic waters, escaping only to the slightly more temperate waters towards the Arctic Circle in the dead of winter, but never entering the warmer southern seas. In summer the hunters of Thule are fortunate to witness the annual return of the narwhal to the Inglefield Fjord, on the side of which we now sat.

The narwhal ... is an essential contributor to the survival of the hunters in the High Arctic. The mattak or blubber of the whale is rich in necessary minerals and vitamins, and in a place where the climate prohibits the growth of vegetables or fruit, this rich source of vitamin C was the one reason that the Eskimos have never suffered from scurvy. ... For centuries the blubber of the whales was also the only source of light and heat, and the dark rich meat is still a valuable part of the diet for both man and dogs (a single narwhal can feed a team of dogs for an entire month). Its single ivory tusk, which can grow up to six feet in length, was used for harpoon tips and handles for other hunting implements (although the ivory was found to be brittle and not hugely satisfactory as a weapon), for carving protective tupilaks, and even as a central beam for their small ancient dwellings. Strangely, the tusk seems to have little use for the narwhal itself; they do not use the tusk to break through ice as a breathing hole, nor will they use it to catch or attack prey, but rather the primary use seems to be to disturb the top of the sea bed in order to catch Arctic halibut for which they have a particular predilection. Often the ends of their tusks are worn down or even broken from such usage.

The women clustered on the knoll of the lookout, binoculars pointing in every direction, each woman focusing on her husband or family member, occasionally spinning round at a small gasp or jump as one of the women saw a hunter near a narwhal. ... Each wife knew her husband instinctively and watched their progress intently; it was crucial to her that her husband catch a narwhal — it was part of their staple diet, and some of the mattak and meat could be sold to other hunters who hadn't been so lucky, bringing in some much-needed extra income. Every hunter was on the water. It was like watching a vast, waterborne game with the hunters spread like a net around the sound.

The narwhal ... are intelligent creatures, their senses are keen and they talk to one another under the water. Their hearing is particularly developed and they can hear the sound of a paddling kayak from a great distance. That ... was why the hunters had to sit so very still in the water.

One hunter was almost on top of a pair of narwhal, and they were huge. He gently picked up his harpoon and aimed — in that split second my heart leapt for both hunter and narwhal. I urged the man on in my head; he was so close, and so brave to attempt what he was about to do — he was miles from land in a flimsy kayak, and could easily be capsized and drowned. The hunter had no rifle, only one harpoon with two heads and one bladder. It was a foolhardy exercise and one that could only inspire respect. And yet at the same time my heart also urged the narwhal to dive, to leave, to survive.

This dilemma stayed with me the whole time that I was in Greenland. I understand the harshness of life in the Arctic and the needs of the hunters and their families to hunt and live on animals and sea mammals that we demand to be protected because of their beauty. And I know that one cannot afford to be sentimental in the Arctic. 'How can you possibly eat seal?' I have been asked over and over again. True, the images that bombarded us several years ago of men battering seals for their fur hasn't helped the issue of polar hunting, but the Inughuit do not kill seals using this method, nor do they kill for sport. They use every part of the animals they kill, and most of the food in Thule is still brought in by the hunter-gatherers and fishermen. Imported goods can only ever account for part of the food supply; there is still only one annual supply ship that makes it through the ice to Qaanaaq, and the small twice-weekly plane from West Greenland can only carry a certain amount of goods. Hunting is still an absolute necessity in Thule.

spectral-play.quote: the plumes of spray from the narwhal catching the light in a spectral play of colour
spectral-play.what: 'Spectral' suggests ghostly, otherworldly beauty. Creates ethereal atmosphere.
spectral-play.effect: Transforms hunting scene into something magical, not brutal. Sets tone of wonder.

two-pods.quote: Two large pods of narwhal circled in the fjord, often looking as if they were going to merge, but always slowly, methodically passing each other by
two-pods.what: Describes whale movement like a dance - 'methodically' suggests deliberate pattern.
two-pods.effect: Creates sense of natural rhythm and order, almost ceremonial quality to the scene.

glittering-kingdom.what: Arctic becomes a magical kingdom, suggesting royalty and treasure.
glittering-kingdom.effect: Elevates the Arctic from harsh wasteland to magnificent realm worth protecting.

sharp-intake.quote: took a sharp intake of breath
sharp-intake.what: Shows involuntary physical response to beauty of scene.
sharp-intake.effect: Makes reader feel her awe. Shows she's still capable of being moved despite familiarity.

butter-gold.quote: The evening light was turning butter-gold, glinting off man and whale and catching the soft billows of smoke from a lone hunter's pipe
butter-gold.what: Rich visual imagery with 'butter-gold' suggesting warmth and richness.
butter-gold.effect: Creates painterly scene. Links hunter and whale in same golden light - both part of nature.

close-enough.quote: From where we sat at the lookout it looked as though the hunters were close enough to touch the narwhal with their bare hands and yet they never moved
close-enough.what: Emphasises stillness and patience of hunters. Distance deceives the eye.
close-enough.effect: Shows discipline of hunters. Creates tension - so close yet requiring perfect stillness.

distances-deceptive.quote: Distances are always deceptive in the Arctic
distances-deceptive.what: Direct statement educating readers about Arctic conditions.
distances-deceptive.effect: Reminds readers this is alien environment with different rules. Nothing is as it seems.

fell-wondering.quote: I fell to wondering if the narwhal existed at all or were instead mischievous tricks of the shifting light
fell-wondering.what: 'Mischievous tricks' personifies light. Questions reality itself.
fell-wondering.effect: Creates dreamlike quality. Shows how Arctic can make you question your senses.

rarely-stray.quote: The narwhal rarely stray from High Arctic waters
rarely-stray.what: Shifts to informative mode, explaining narwhal behaviour.
rarely-stray.effect: Establishes narwhal as truly Arctic creatures - they belong here, nowhere else.

hunters-fortunate.quote: the hunters of Thule are fortunate to witness the annual return of the narwhal to the Inglefield Fjord
hunters-fortunate.what: 'Fortunate' frames hunting positively - as privilege not exploitation.
hunters-fortunate.effect: Reframes hunting as respectful observation of natural cycles, not domination.

essential-contributor.quote: The narwhal ... is an essential contributor to the survival of the hunters in the High Arctic
essential-contributor.what: 'Essential contributor' makes narwhal active participant in Arctic life.
essential-contributor.effect: Not just food but 'contributor' - suggests reciprocal relationship, not exploitation.

rich-minerals.quote: rich in necessary minerals and vitamins
rich-minerals.what: Scientific language validates importance with facts.
rich-minerals.effect: Appeals to logic - this isn't preference but biological necessity.

climate-prohibits.quote: in a place where the climate prohibits the growth of vegetables or fruit, this rich source of vitamin C was the one reason that the Eskimos have never suffered from scurvy
climate-prohibits.what: Explains that narwhal literally prevented disease and death.
climate-prohibits.effect: Shows hunting as medical necessity - without it, people would have died of scurvy.

for-centuries.quote: For centuries the blubber of the whales was also the only source of light and heat
for-centuries.what: Time marker 'for centuries' shows long tradition.
for-centuries.effect: This isn't new exploitation but ancient sustainable practice.

valuable-diet.quote: the dark rich meat is still a valuable part of the diet for both man and dogs (a single narwhal can feed a team of dogs for an entire month)
valuable-diet.what: Specific detail about feeding dogs for a month shows practical value.
valuable-diet.effect: Concrete example makes abstract necessity real and measurable.

ivory-tusk.quote: Its single ivory tusk, which can grow up to six feet in length
ivory-tusk.effect: Shows magnificence of creature while explaining practical uses.

strangely-tusk.quote: Strangely, the tusk seems to have little use for the narwhal itself
strangely-tusk.what: 'Strangely' shows her curiosity about nature's design.
strangely-tusk.effect: Adds element of mystery - even the narwhal's defining feature puzzles us.

worn-broken.quote: Often the ends of their tusks are worn down or even broken from such usage
worn-broken.what: Physical evidence supports theory about tusk use.
worn-broken.effect: Shows narwhals as active creatures using their tusks, not just display.

women-clustered.quote: The women clustered on the knoll of the lookout, binoculars pointing in every direction
women-clustered.what: Shifts focus to women's experience of the hunt.
women-clustered.effect: Shows hunt affects whole community, not just hunters. Women's anxiety palpable.

each-woman.quote: each woman focusing on her husband or family member, occasionally spinning round at a small gasp or jump as one of the women saw a hunter near a narwhal
each-woman.what: Details of gasps and jumps show nervous energy.
each-woman.effect: Creates tension through women's reactions. Humanises the watching and waiting.

knew-instinctively.quote: Each wife knew her husband instinctively and watched their progress intently
knew-instinctively.effect: Emphasises human relationships at stake - not just abstract hunting but families.

crucial-catch.quote: it was crucial to her that her husband catch a narwhal — it was part of their staple diet, and some of the mattak and meat could be sold to other hunters who hadn't been so lucky, bringing in some much-needed extra income
crucial-catch.what: Explains financial as well as nutritional importance.
crucial-catch.effect: Shows modern economic pressures alongside traditional needs.

waterborne-game.quote: It was like watching a vast, waterborne game with the hunters spread like a net around the sound
waterborne-game.what: Hunt compared to strategic game with hunters as net.
waterborne-game.effect: Shows organisation and strategy, not random violence. 'Game' suggests rules and skill.

intelligent-creatures.quote: The narwhal ... are intelligent creatures, their senses are keen and they talk to one another under the water
intelligent-creatures.effect: Makes killing them more morally complex - these aren't dumb animals but thinking beings.

hearing-developed.quote: Their hearing is particularly developed and they can hear the sound of a paddling kayak from a great distance
hearing-developed.effect: Shows hunt isn't easy - narwhals have advantages, making it more fair contest.

why-still.quote: That ... was why the hunters had to sit so very still in the water
why-still.what: Links back to earlier observation about stillness.
why-still.effect: Everything connects - the stillness now makes sense given narwhal hearing.

split-second.quote: in that split second my heart leapt for both hunter and narwhal
split-second.what: Heart 'leaping' for both shows emotional division.
split-second.effect: Central moment of moral conflict - can't choose sides.

urged-on.quote: I urged the man on in my head
urged-on.what: Internal cheering for hunter shows cultural allegiance.
urged-on.effect: Despite conflict, her first instinct supports the hunter.

brave-attempt.quote: he was so close, and so brave to attempt what he was about to do — he was miles from land in a flimsy kayak, and could easily be capsized and drowned
brave-attempt.what: Details the real danger to hunter - this isn't safe or easy.
brave-attempt.effect: Hunter risks his life - not casual killing but dangerous necessity.

no-rifle.quote: The hunter had no rifle, only one harpoon with two heads and one bladder
no-rifle.what: Emphasises traditional, not modern hunting methods.
no-rifle.effect: More equal contest - no modern advantages, just skill and courage.

foolhardy-respect.quote: It was a foolhardy exercise and one that could only inspire respect
foolhardy-respect.effect: Complex response - thinks it's crazy but respects the courage required.

yet-same-time.quote: And yet at the same time my heart also urged the narwhal to dive, to leave, to survive
yet-same-time.what: Major turning point with 'And yet' showing other side of feeling.
yet-same-time.effect: Perfect balance - equal sympathy for hunter and hunted.

dilemma-stayed.quote: This dilemma stayed with me the whole time that I was in Greenland
dilemma-stayed.what: Shows this isn't momentary but ongoing moral struggle.
dilemma-stayed.effect: Not easily resolved - the conflict persists and troubles her.

understand-harshness.quote: I understand the harshness of life in the Arctic and the needs of the hunters and their families to hunt and live on animals and sea mammals that we demand to be protected because of their beauty
understand-harshness.what: Directly addresses Western protectionist attitudes versus Arctic reality.
understand-harshness.effect: Shows Western hypocrisy - we protect for beauty while they need for survival.

cannot-sentimental.quote: And I know that one cannot afford to be sentimental in the Arctic
cannot-sentimental.what: Firm statement about emotional luxury versus survival.
cannot-sentimental.effect: Sentimentality is privilege of the comfortable - Arctic doesn't allow it.

how-eat-seal.quote: 'How can you possibly eat seal?' I have been asked over and over again
how-eat-seal.what: Direct quote of repeated criticism she faces.
how-eat-seal.effect: Shows she's caught between worlds - defending one to the other.

true-images.quote: True, the images that bombarded us several years ago of men battering seals for their fur hasn't helped the issue of polar hunting
true-images.what: Admits negative media has damaged perception.
true-images.effect: Shows awareness of why people object while preparing counter-argument.

not-kill-method.quote: but the Inughuit do not kill seals using this method, nor do they kill for sport
not-kill-method.what: Clearly distinguishes Inughuit from commercial hunters.
not-kill-method.effect: Not all hunting is the same - this is subsistence not commercial exploitation.

use-every-part.quote: They use every part of the animals they kill
use-every-part.effect: Shows respect for life taken - opposite of wasteful Western consumption.

food-brought.quote: most of the food in Thule is still brought in by the hunter-gatherers and fishermen
food-brought.what: 'Still' emphasises this continues today, not just history.
food-brought.effect: This isn't museum culture but living necessity.

imported-goods.quote: Imported goods can only ever account for part of the food supply; there is still only one annual supply ship that makes it through the ice to Qaanaaq, and the small twice-weekly plane from West Greenland can only carry a certain amount of goods
imported-goods.effect: Shows it's literally impossible to live on imported food - geography prevents it.

absolute-necessity.quote: Hunting is still an absolute necessity in Thule
absolute-necessity.what: Definitive final statement using 'absolute' for emphasis.
absolute-necessity.effect: No ambiguity - after showing both sides, concludes hunting must continue.

mattak.meaning: The fatty skin/blubber of the whale
mattak.note: Inughuit word for whale blubber, rich in vitamins and minerals essential for Arctic survival.
mattak.effect: Using indigenous term shows respect for culture and emphasises this is traditional practice.

tupilaks.meaning: Magical figures or charms with protective powers
tupilaks.note: Traditional Inuit carved figures believed to have spiritual/magical properties.
tupilaks.effect: Shows spiritual dimension of narwhal use - not just physical but cultural/religious importance.

predilection.meaning: A preference or special liking for something
predilection.note: From Latin meaning 'to choose beforehand' - indicates the narwhal's particular fondness for halibut.
predilection.effect: Scientific vocabulary adds authority to observations about narwhal behavior.

overview.heading: Why Herbert Wrote This
overview.intro: Herbert's purposes evolve through the passage:

points.label: To explain Arctic survival
points.text: "The narwhal is an essential contributor to the survival" - Shows hunting is necessity, not choice

points.label: To challenge Western assumptions
points.text: "How can you possibly eat seal?" - Addresses Western criticism directly

points.label: To share moral complexity
points.text: "This dilemma stayed with me" - Shows her own conflicted feelings

points.label: Western readers unfamiliar with Arctic life
points.text: "Distances are always deceptive in the Arctic" - Educates about environment

points.label: Critics of Arctic hunting
points.text: "I have been asked over and over again" - Responds to common criticisms

points.label: Those seeking understanding
points.text: Detailed explanations of narwhal uses - For genuinely curious readers

points.label: Wonder and awe
points.text: "took a sharp intake of breath" - Childlike amazement at beauty

points.label: Informative teacher
points.text: "The narwhal are intelligent creatures" - Educational, factual tone

points.label: Conflicted observer
points.text: "my heart leapt for both hunter and narwhal" - Torn between cultures

points.label: Defensive advocate
points.text: "one cannot afford to be sentimental" - Firm, protective of Inughuit

points.label: Magical imagery
points.text: "spectral play of colour", "glittering kingdom" - Fairytale quality

points.label: Sensory description
points.text: "butter-gold light glinting" - Rich visual and tactile imagery

points.label: Metaphor
points.text: "vast, waterborne game" - Hunt as strategic game

points.label: Beauty to necessity
points.text: Opens with magical description, moves to survival needs

points.label: Pivotal moment
points.text: "And yet at the same time" - Turning point revealing conflict

points.label: Circular resolution
points.text: "This dilemma stayed with me" to "absolute necessity" - Returns to defend hunting

points.label: Final emphasis
points.text: "Hunting is still an absolute necessity" - Conclusive statement
